content.title: Stream It Or Skip It: 'UNTOLD: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom' on Netflix, a Documentary Look at the Sordid and Almost Tragic Past of an NBA star and Tabloid Icon

Please Try Again. Powered by Reelgood Lamar Odom was an NBA star — a key piece on two championship teams and a Sixth Man of the Year Award winner. His fame went beyond the court, though, with a tabloid marriage to reality star Khloe Kardashian making him a household name. The headlines turned darker, though, when a near-fatal series of strokes in a Nevada brothel nearly cost him his life. UNTOLD: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom, a new feature-length entry in Netflix’s ongoing documentary series, follows Odom’s life, career, spiral and subsequent recovery. UNTOLD: THE DEATH AND LIFE OF LAMAR ODOM: STREAM IT OR SKIP IT? The Gist: Even if you’re not a basketball fan, you’ve probably heard Lamar Odom’s name. He was a good basketball player, to be clear — a key part of two championship teams, a consistent performer across fourteen NBA seasons — but that’s not why I’m confident you’ve heard of him. His 2009 marriage to reality-TV star Khloe Kardashian — after a month of dating — rocketed him onto tabloid headlines and into late-night monologues. The pressures of fame quickly spiraled into dangerous territory, and Odom hit rock bottom with a near-fatal series of strokes following a drug overdose in a Nevada brothel in 2015. UNTOLD: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom tracks a bit of Odom’s early life, but focuses most on his days as a Los Angeles Laker and Kardashian-adjacent celebrity. This brings in a lot of familiar faces: former Lakers head coach Phil Jackson and teammate Ron Artest, ex-wife Khloe and more. Their testimonies are interwoven with game highlights, news clips and other contemporaneous fragments of Odom’s peak moment, leading up to his precipitous fall and near death. Photo: Getty Images What Movies Will It Remind You Of? Netflix has established a consistent brand with the UNTOLD series, with six volumes and twenty-and-counting documentaries under their belt. The Death and Life of Lamar Odom hews to this formula, and recalls some of the better ones that came before it. Those include other rise-and-fall athlete dramas such as UNTOLD: Johnny Football, UNTOLD: The Fall of Favre, and UNTOLD: The Murder of Air McNair — the latter a reminder of how much darker Odom’s story could’ve turned out. Performance Worth Watching: Odom himself being here is critical to the documentary’s success, but some of the most compelling (and difficult) testimony comes from his ex-girlfriend and mother of his first three children Liza Morales, who tearfully recalls the loss of one of their children to Sudden Infant Death Syndrome. On a much lighter front, the presence of Odom’s former Laker teammate Ron Artest keeps things lively. “I think we drove Kobe crazy,” Artest laughs at one point, recalls the dysfunction of the late-aughts Lakers. “I’m rapping, Lamar’s doing reality shows… but we came to practice!” Sex And Skin: Nothing directly, but, considering the first two minutes discuss Odom’s near-fatal overdose in a Nevada brothel, I think we can comfortably consider this an “adults only” watch. Photo: Netflix Our Take: Can I start with a hot take here? (Of course I can, that’s a hypothetical question.) Okay, here’s my hot take: I think that Phil Jackson is one of the luckiest head coaches in NBA history. That’s probably heresy, as Jackson is widely celebrated for his NBA-record 11 championships, a level of success that’s famously attributed to his “Zen Master” approach to coaching. Of course, it’s a lot easier to be zen when you’ve got Jordan, Shaq and Kobe leading your teams. (They say there are no atheists in foxholes, and there’s no zen masters coaching the Sacramento Kings.) I digress, of course, but it’s hard not to when Jackson pops in to The Death and Life of Lamar Odom with some lofty talk of zen koans that just makes it seem like his real superpower was not paying too much attention to his superstar-powered teams. The documentary, the latest in Netflix’s now-well-established sports-doc imprint, promises to focus on the life and career of the star-crossed former Lakers star, but it takes a pretty quick path to the 2009-2015 window when Odom became a side character on Keeping Up With the Kardashians–and then nearly died after a drug overdose in a Nevada brothel. [Phil Jackson voice] ommmm If you followed Odom’s Kardashian saga as it happened, then you’re not going to be surprised by any of the details of his spiral. What makes The Death and Life of Lamar Odom compelling is that he’s still here to talk about it. Heck, I’ll confess. When I first saw the title a few weeks ago, I momentarily blanked and thought he had died. That’s on me, but given the depths he sank to, it certainly wasn’t out of the question. To Kardashian’s credit–and, let’s be clear, despite her family’s fame-seeking, Khloe was treated pretty awful by the media–she comes across as level-headed and sympathetic in her extensive interviews in the documentary, much as Odom comes across as having been changed by his experiences. This might’ve been a circus as it happened, but there appears to be genuine growth and recovery on display now. It’s that growth that keeps The Death and Life of Lamar Odom from feeling like a reality show itself, and instead being a genuinely worthwhile watch. Our Call: STREAM IT. Netflix has managed to deliver consistently strong documentaries under the UNTOLD banner, and The Death and Life of Lamar Odom gives them plenty of story to work with. Scott Hines is a Louisville, Kentucky-based writer and publisher of the much-loved Action Cookbook Newsletter.
